articles.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
articles.summary:
I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.
To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers.
Things that were fun to get right:
- Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes.
- Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities.
- Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.
Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.
Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

articles.title: This Week in Package Management: 7 November 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me. Version control and forge news is in the Wednesday This Week in Source Control roundup.
Security
Vox Pupuli fixed three critical vulnerabilities that a Neodyme researcher reported in OpenVox, the community fork of Puppet. OpenVox Server deserialised Ruby objects embedded in agent run reports, which allowed remote code execution. The shared Trapperkeeper authorisation library matched every plain-string rule in auth.conf as a wildcard, so a certificate for evil.target.example.com was accepted as target.example.com. The OpenVoxDB container image allowed any certificate to reach its API because its allowlist script failed on startup.
All known Puppet implementations are affected, and the fixes are in openvox-agent 8.32.0 and 9.3.0 and openvox-server and openvoxdb 8.18.0 and 9.2.0. Updates to open source Puppet, including security fixes, have ended, so Vox Pupuli recommends migrating to OpenVox.
An issue on actions/runner-images reports that GitHub’s public macOS runners still accept certificates from the compromised eMudhra intermediates covered here last week. Apple has yet to patch the system /etc/ssl/cert.pem. Homebrew has shipped patched ca-certificates, curl and git, but the runner images disable Homebrew updates, so jobs run the vulnerable preinstalled versions.
DSA-6607-1 fixes CVE-2026-109518 in APT, found by Max Justicz. When an HTTP redirect gave two package downloads the same URI, APT could merge them. A retried download then let an attacker on the network path, including a malicious mirror or proxy, replace a package after verification and run code as root.
The attack needs Acquire::Retries set to 1 or higher, and the default is 3 from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04. Fixed versions are 3.0.4 for trixie, 2.6.2 for bookworm and 3.3.6 in unstable.
A Nixpkgs advisory covers two bugs in darwin.linux-builder, the Linux VM that macOS users run as a remote builder. The run-builder script added the whole keys directory to the world-readable Nix store, so any local user could log in as builder, a trusted user on the VM’s Nix daemon (GHSA-45qr-47fw-2p57).
The QEMU variants also forwarded the builder’s SSH port on every network interface (GHSA-w5j5-2jpq-3cv3). Fixes are on unstable and 26.05, and after updating the advisory says to delete the old key pair from the store, regenerate it and delete the builder’s disk image.
Docker Engine 29.9.3 fixes four CVEs in the engine and SwarmKit. It also updates to BuildKit 0.34.2, which fixes a resolver cache poisoning crash when a build resolves the same Git source twice.
Releases
hex.pm opened Workload Identity and staged publishing to every package and organisation. A GitHub Actions job can exchange its OIDC token for a Workload Identity token that expires after 15 minutes and can publish only that package. An organisation can also use a read identity to fetch its private packages in CI with only the job’s OIDC token. Staged publishing holds releases published with a key or a workload identity until a person approves them with a fresh 2FA code.
New packages get staging by default and existing packages have to opt in. Staged releases expire after seven days. Hex 2.7.0 adds mix hex.publish --wait, which blocks until the release is approved and exits with an error if it is rejected or expires. A new --check-unused-ignores flag makes mix hex.audit fail on ignore entries that match nothing in mix.lock.
PyPI’s redesigned project pages add a Security tab that shows each release’s provenance and the attestations for each file. A release counts as having full provenance only when every file has a Trusted Publisher or SLSA build attestation. Warnings flag incomplete, inconsistent, changed or lost provenance, and files uploaded more than 14 days after an older release get a late-upload marker.
conda 26.10.0 makes conda-rattler-solver the default solver, including after upgrades where the solver setting is unset. --solver=libmamba selects the libmamba solver, and the classic pycosat solver now ships in a bundled conda-pycosat-solver plugin. The release also records when an environment was last activated and adds --disable-plugins and --enable-plugins for switching individual plugins off and on.
pnpm 12.18.0 publishes platform variants of a package to pnpr registries as one archive per target, and installs the variant that fits the host. Publishing to any other registry requires --no-variants, which publishes only the archive that targets any platform. Agent skills are now approved one skill at a time and linked under their own names. pnpr 0.1.0-alpha.18 stores hosted package metadata in SQLite or libSQL and logs release records in transparency logs.
mise 2026.11.0 (now 2026.11.3) makes --locked require checksums, and safe mode now ignores project lockfiles. It adds opt-in Sigstore provenance verification for npm: tools, which checks only the tool’s own package and requires the embedded aube package manager. Tasks can now declare a lock so that runs sharing a database or simulator execute one at a time, even across worktrees.
pixi 0.84.0 (now 0.84.1) moves exclude-newer into the [workspace] table and supports exemptions to the cutoff. A workspace can apply the cutoff to new releases by default and exempt vetted security releases. A rattler fix for hash collisions between unequal package versions means lockfiles written by older pixi versions may require a pixi lock before pixi accepts them as locked.
pip 26.3 blocks unexpected imports during installation and warns about unsafe ones afterwards. HTTP redirects to file: URLs are now rejected, and PyPI’s restriction on direct URL dependencies now covers extras and cached wheels. -r pylock.toml now supports extras and non-default dependency groups, and accepts --no-binary. The security policy now states that installing untrusted wheels has always been unsafe, since Python’s import system can run third-party code during installation.
Gradle 9.9.0 promotes the custom dependencies block API out of incubation, including bundles and constraints from providers. When the wrapper task regenerates gradle-wrapper.properties, it now carries over existing settings such as distribution type, timeouts and retries. It still regenerates distributionUrl, which overwrites a custom host.
zizmor 1.32.0 adds experimental support for GitHub’s new workflow lockfiles. It now collects only the inputs GitHub Actions reads, so it skips workflows in vendored directories.
Renovate 44.210.0 to 44.222.0 adds a julia manager with a datasource for the General registry and Julia versioning, and reads transitive dependencies from uv.lock for security updates. Extracted constraints are now shared across managers. A tool version pinned in mise or rust-toolchain limits the updates other managers open.
Dependabot version updates now support Microsoft’s Agent Package Manager on github.com, following the apm ecosystem added in Dependabot Core 0.400.0. It opens pull requests for git dependencies declared in apm.yml and regenerates apm.lock.yaml when present. The support covers version updates only.

Articles
Friction in the Python Packaging Standards Process (konsti, uv) lists problems with how packaging PEPs get made. The text goes through editing passes before and after discussion and moves between reStructuredText and Markdown. Discussions on discuss.python.org have no concern tracking, and several maintainers avoid the forum. Small changes, such as removing a decade-old unimplemented feature, require a full PEP. The post points to Rust’s RFC concern tracking and final comment period as prior art.
Scrutinize our assessments (Daniel Stenberg) follows up on curl moving low and medium severity vulnerability handling into public GitHub issues. Stenberg explains the vuln:ASSESS, vuln:NONE, vuln:LOW and vuln:MEDIUM labels and asks outsiders to challenge the severity calls. CVE IDs are visible from assignment, and the full records are published on the release date.
The author of No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem” (smoores.dev) hit npm’s typosquat check while naming a package for the Storyteller project. The registry rejected estee as too similar to espree and testem, then flagged the fallback hoid against hoek, hono, uuid and zod. npm support declined to lift the automated block. The author infers an edit-distance-of-two rule against popular names. Under that rule preact and estree would also be blocked.
The intensional model in disguise (Farid Zakaria) maps Nix onto Bazel and buck2. Bazel and buck2 key actions by the content of their inputs, so editing a comment in a C file stops the rebuild once the compiled output comes out the same. Nix gets that early cutoff only with content-addressed derivations, because by default it addresses outputs by their recipe. The post lines up Nix’s resolved derivations, realisations and store with Bazel’s actions, action cache and CAS.
Josh Bressers talked to Roi Nisimi about backport gaps: security fixes merged to a project’s main branch but missing from its latest release. Nisimi’s write-up for Orca Security reports hundreds of confirmed cases from a scan of thousands of repositories. Advisories and published vulnerable ranges are often missing for these fixes, so scanners report the current release as clean.
Elsewhere
DCFinder (Xiaoya Zhu et al., Journal of Computer Security) detects dependency confusion in Python projects that use more than one index. It builds the transitive tree from private indexes and PyPI and checks whether the resolver would select a public version. On 28 real projects it reports 88.7% precision and 83.3% recall, against zero detections from the baseline tools.
Vlad Miricioiu, director of the Software Stewardship Lab and one of my FOSDEM devroom co-organisers, talked to RedMonk about binary dependencies, maintainer burnout, funding models and the Bernies. The Stewardship Lab received $5,000 from Syntax and Sentry towards an annual survey of burnout among open source maintainers.
Software Line Specialist (Lovro Bikić) is a delightful bit of satire.

articles.title: Ask HN: How did you convince family and friends to join your XMPP/Matrix server?
articles.summary:
I love open-source software and open protocols, but my family and friends primarily communicate through SMS for exactly the reasons in https://xkcd.com/2365/
Whenever XMPP or Matrix threads pop up on HN, several commenters casually mention their "friends and family XMPP (or Matrix) server."
How did you convince friends and family to move away from SMS/WhatsApp and replace it with a niche messaging app?
My family and friends aren't hardcore nerdy, but they're more tech-savvy than average. Their needs in messaging are mainly pragmatic: they want ease of use, reliability, and fun features. They don't care that much about privacy, decentralization, or extensibility (though I care about those things a lot).
I've been experimenting with self-hosting XMPP and Matrix servers and clients in the past week, and the UX is even worse than I expected. It seems like all the clients either imitate Slack, imitate Discord, or imitate hot garbage. I haven't seen any that try to be a simple, friendly replacement for SMS. I'm a software developer who uses computers all day, and I find the UX for most of the clients incredibly hard to use.
The only angle I could see to pitch XMPP/Matrix to people for non-philosophical reasons are that there's a more consistent experience across iOS/Android. The biggest shortcoming I think is visible to regular users is that there's feature degradation and missing information when iOS users have SMS conversations with Android users, especially in group chats.
For people who have successfully won family and friends to XMPP or Matrix, what was your pitch? What do you recommend others do to make XMPP or Matrix an attractive experience for a regular person?

JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine's "Against Tech Oligarchy" (permalink) JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine are veterans of a string of hard-fought unionization drives at tech workplaces that started with some astounding successes but ran up against ferocious resistance in the second Trump term; their book about tech labor, Against Tech Oligarchy, is a superb analysis of the challenges and potential for tech labor organizing: https://againsttecholigarchy.com/ For decades, tech workers enjoyed extraordinary power, despite the fact that virtually no tech workers were in unions. That's because tech workers were both extremely valuable to their employers (each engineer hired by a Silicon Valley firm added about $1m to the company's bottom line) and extremely scarce. This won tech workers very favorable working conditions, high compensation, and a great deal of control over their employers' products (because if a worker refused to work on a project, it was hard to find someone else to do the work). What's more, there has always been a sizable cohort of tech workers whose own lives were profoundly improved by access to digital networks and wanted more than anything to distribute those benefits to everyone else. I call these workers "Tron-pilled," because they fought for the user: https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/11/obvious-terrible-ideas/#bayesian-terrorism During the era of tech worker scarcity, few tech workers saw themselves as workers at all – rather, the tech worker's self-conception was as an entrepreneur in waiting, a temporarily embarrassed founder. Tech bosses played on this perception, promoting the idea of tech workers and managers as peers and/or family members. Tech CEOs affected hoodies and jeans and hosted company-wide meetings where they allowed engineers to pepper them with impertinent questions about the company's technical and commercial direction. But scarcity-based power only lasts until supply catches up with demand. As the number of workers outstripped the number of jobs, bosses showed their true colors. That's what happened at Kickstarter, when one of the bosses forced out his co-founders and declared himself CEO and proceeded to override the decisions of the company's Trust and Safety team. This sparked one of tech's first unionization drives, and it was a bitter fight, with management pulling out every dirty tactic in the union-busting playbook: https://kickstarterunited.org/oral-history/ The labor militancy at Kickstarter United wasn't an isolated incident. Workers at much bigger companies like Google and Microsoft had a long tradition of pushing back against management through internal channels, open letters, and, starting in 2018, mass walkouts: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Google_walkouts But post-Trump, bosses at these companies were much less willing to countenance dissent, and waves of vicious retaliation and reprisals radicalized many workers at these companies, driving them to more traditional, organized forms of labor activism. At the same time, workers at smaller, "mission-driven" shops like Bandcamp were inspired by the success of Kickstarter United and they started their own drives. All this attracted the interest of the "internationals" – big, established unions like the Communications Workers of America – who trained union organizers at all kinds of tech shops and started laying the groundwork for traditional union drives. Most of Against Tech Oligarchy tells the story of these drives in a gripping you-are-there style (it helps that both of the authors are veterans of several of these campaigns). The stakes get much higher during the pandemic, of course, as tech comes to play a more central role in the lives of hundreds of millions of locked-down workers, and as the tech companies themselves went on uncontrolled hiring sprees, putting workers on the payroll without any duties or responsibilities, often just to ensure that a rival company couldn't hire them. The pandemic also prompted many tech bosses to express far more worker-hostile sentiments than they'd ever let slip in public before. Fully remote workforces both frustrated tech bosses and also significantly reduced the opportunities for in-person labor organizing. All of this built to a series of rising crescendos, such as Musk's Twitter takeover and mass layoffs, and Israel's tech-fueled genocide in Gaza. Confrontations between tech workers and bosses grew more bitter and direct, even as solidarity between white-collar tech workers and their blue-collar peers (notably Amazon warehouse workers) increased. If all Against Tech Oligarchy did was lay out the cut-and-thrust of these labor struggles during these momentous years, it would be worth the price of admission. But it's in the final chapters that the book really distinguishes itself, because it's here that the authors embark on a pitiless postmortem of their own failed campaigns and the failures of their peers and ask themselves what it will take to unionize tech workers. They start with the observation that most American union organizing is built around maintaining "labor peace" (by swiftly moving to recognition and a contract) but that tech bosses are ready to wage "labor war" (through illegal union-busting and retaliation). A labor peace strategy avoids costly and dangerous risks to established unions, such as decertification of locals and expensive and bruising court battles. But for tech bosses, labor war pays off, because their workforce is transient, fragmented, and skeptical of the very idea that they are workers. They have little to no experience with unions and can barely imagine how a union might improve their working lives. The traditional labor playbook calls for workers to quietly build their power, taking no overt action while conducting a series of personal, one-to-one conversations that contribute to an eventual quorum of workers that's large enough to win a unionization vote. This strategy is like building a bonfire, where the pieces of fuel are piled one atop the other, but not lit until the pile is done. But in a tech shop where workers turn over frequently and work in isolated teams, often from home, this strategy fails. Workers who have been won to the union side leave or grow demoralized in their isolation. Reaching new workers is difficult, and since the whole union drive occurs in secret, new workers don't know to reach out to organizers in their shops. For Tan and Redwine, this fact militates for a strategy that revives some of the pre-labor activism of tech workers, noisy public/private fights whenever product decisions and management conduct violates some mix of worker rights and workers' values. They see this as a way to build momentum within a shop, bringing workers off the sidelines and giving organizers chances to bring those workers into a sustained, structured labor drive. Tan and Redwine see tech worker organizing as the frontrunners of an age of new labor militancy and labor war, of the sort that pre-dated the labor peace that arose after the passage of the National Labor Relations Act. That labor peace was the result of bosses learning that hardball tactics would be met with equally hardcore responses. This is especially important for tech workers, whose strikes cannot inflict the same pain on their bosses as earlier industrial workers' strikes did. Digital systems are designed to operate themselves after their are built, so when the workers involved in those systems withdraw their labor, the systems continue to run, often for a very long time, before needing maintenance (this is also the lesson of Musk's mass layoffs at Twitter). Tech bosses have metabolized this lesson, and they are increasingly willing to wage all-out war at the first sign of labor unrest, with waves of retaliatory firings. These bosses have figured out devilish tactics for constructive dismissal, like the CEO of Mapbox, who retaliated against union supporters by targeting them with "return to office" mandates that forced them to report in person to offices that were in distant states. This prompted many of these workers to quit, which spared Mapbox from even paying them a severance package. Against this backdrop, strikes need to be seen not as a way to bring the business operations to a halt, but rather as a way to galvanize workers and bring them into the union drive. As New York Times Tech Guild organizer John Cruickshank put it, Action builds capacity for action. This is the ethos of the Microsoft workers who have campaigned tirelessly to halt the company's participation in the genocide in Gaza. They barricaded themselves in executives' offices, livestreaming the confrontation; they disrupted Microsoft's livecast 50th anniversary celebration; and they paddled a flotilla of protest kayaks outside of top Microsoft executives' waterfront homes. All of this paid off, with Microsoft halting sales of its tools to a particularly notorious unit of the Israeli military who had been using the company's products to conduct surveillance in Gaza and the West Bank. Tan and Redwine see these novel tactics as a rewilding of the labor movement, a return to the militant roots that led to the labor peace, but only after all-out labor war. They cite the 1934 Minneapolis truck drivers' strike, where workers invented the "flying picket" by swarming scab trucks far from the factory gates, defeating the trucks' police protection, which led to a general strike and a total victory for labor. This is important historical context. The genteel business of getting everyone's cards signed and having the NLRB certify your union was the compromise bosses agreed to after they learned that the alternative was far worse for them. Today, it's not just bosses who've forgotten that lesson – many workers have, too. Against Tech Oligarchy aims to rekindle those old boilers and get the unstoppable labor train running again.
